No. 22· 5 November 2026· Global, Italy in focus· Illustrated edition
In three lines

  1. Kimberly-Clark closes its $48.7 billion acquisition of Kenvue on November 2, creating a ten-billion-dollar-brand health and wellness group and putting a Mondelez alum in the CMO chair: the whole deal is about owning brands outright, not renting anyone's fame.

  2. Six weeks after Apple quietly broke The Trade Desk's ads in Safari, iOS 27.2 ships October 26 with the fix inside it, but neither company has said on the record that the problem is actually gone.

  3. The data on borrowed fame keeps getting worse: Sydney Sweeney's ads spike web traffic but not sales, while Asiago DOP and Tiffany & Co. both get real mileage out of defending or mining what they already own.

The world

SEC 8-K filings, Kimberly-Clark / Kenvue · November 2, 2026

Kimberly-Clark closes its $48.7 billion purchase of Kenvue, creating a ten-brand health and wellness group

Kimberly-Clark completed its acquisition of Kenvue on November 2: each Kenvue share converted into 0.14625 Kimberly-Clark shares plus $3.50 in cash, an enterprise value of $48.7 billion. The combined company brings together ten billion-dollar-plus brands, including Huggies, Kleenex, Cottonelle and Scott from Kimberly-Clark with Tylenol, Neutrogena, Listerine, Aveeno, Band-Aid and Johnson's from Kenvue, on 2025 combined net revenue of roughly $32 billion and like-for-like operating income near $7 billion. A Global Integration Management Office, staff split about 50/50 between the two companies, is running more than 30 workstreams against a reiterated target of $2.1 billion in run-rate synergies. Marketing now sits under Jonathan Halvorson, who joined Kenvue as chief digital and marketing officer last November after eight years running consumer experience and digital commerce at Mondelez, and now holds the combined group's CMO seat, reporting to chief growth officer Carlos De Jesus.

Why it mattersThis is the Omnicom/Coca-Cola and Salesforce/Braze logic from issue 20, scaled up to the entire personal care aisle: instead of licensing a character or renting a celebrity's current fame, Kimberly-Clark just bought ten brands that already have their own, and put someone whose job is literally "growth" in charge of making them work together.
Apple release notes / ppc.land · shipped October 26, 2026

iOS 27.2 ships with the fix for The Trade Desk's Safari block, six weeks after it first went live

iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 shipped publicly on Monday, October 26, as build 24B119. The update is the one Apple asked The Trade Desk to test on October 5 (issue 21), and which appeared in testing to remove adsrvr.org, The Trade Desk's ad-serving domain, from Safari's private ad-tech blocklist, the same block that had been silently cutting off its ads since iOS 27 shipped September 14 (issues 15-19). As of this issue, no source consulted shows either Apple or The Trade Desk issuing an on-the-record statement confirming the block is actually lifted for ordinary users now that the build is public, only that the fix tested in beta is now the one everyone is running.

Why it mattersA six-week-old ad-serving outage caused by an undocumented private blocklist just quietly disappeared the same way it quietly appeared, through a routine point release rather than a public explanation, which is exactly the opacity issue 21 flagged as the real story here.
laughingplace.com / marketingdive.com / emarketer.com · runs November 4-10, 2026

Disney turns TikTok Shop into a week-long department store for the holidays

Disney's first-ever TikTok Shop "Super Brand Day" runs November 4 through 10, bringing Disney Store together with more than 20 outside brands, including Old Navy, Crocs and Touchland, under one in-app holiday shopping event spanning home, toys, beauty, fashion and accessories built around Disney, Pixar, Marvel and Star Wars gifts. Disney Store opens the event with a TikTok LIVE on November 4. Select items, including a Star Wars "Darth on a Hearth" plush and a Mickey Mouse wreath-themed Loungefly backpack, are TikTok Shop exclusives for the week before arriving on DisneyStore.com on November 11.

Why it mattersDisney isn't just advertising inside TikTok Shop, it's using the app as the actual store for a week, with other retailers riding along inside its event rather than running their own, a different shape of platform dependence than the ad deals this brief usually tracks.
engage.it · campaign launched November 1, 2026 · Il Sole 24 Ore, ruling reported October 2, 2026

Asiago DOP relaunches its name on air weeks after winning its US "Italian sounding" case

The Consorzio Tutela Formaggio Asiago launched "Si, Asiago Dop," a new multichannel campaign, on November 1. It lands five weeks after the Milan Court of Appeal, ruling September 25 on a US dispute, fully overturned a 2023 tribunal decision and sided with the consortium against Giuseppe Citterio Salumificio and Euro Foods over a "Sopressata & Asiago Cheese" product sold in the US that the court found used Italian imagery while containing non-Italian cheese; the ruling bans the product's distribution and awards damages. The consortium's own 2025 figures, filed earlier this year, show origin-level turnover of 181 million euros, up 16.6%.

Why it mattersA protected name only works if someone is willing to spend years in court defending it, and Asiago just did exactly that before spending any money telling consumers to look for the real thing, the opposite order from a brand that advertises first and defends its name later, if ever.

Campaigns & brand moves

contentgrip.com / marketingdive.com / retailgazette.co.uk · campaign live late October 2026

Tiffany & Co. casts Amanda Seyfried in a holiday film built around its own 1965 archive, not a current celebrity moment

"Love Is a Gift," Tiffany's 2026 global holiday campaign with agency American Haiku, centers on a two-minute film directed by Derek Cianfrance starring new house ambassador Amanda Seyfried, set in a fictionalized 1992 and soundtracked by a reimagining of The Wannadies' 1994 "You & Me Song." The ornament at the center of the story is modeled on Jean Schlumberger's 1965 "Bird on a Rock" design, treated as a three-generation keepsake rather than a shopping-list item. American Haiku deliberately moved away from the gloss-and-montage language of typical luxury holiday advertising toward quieter, more intimate performance.

Why it mattersInstead of renting a star's current cultural moment, Tiffany is mining its own sixty-year-old archive and stretching the story back to a period before most of its own target customer was born, betting that a brand's own history reads as more authentic than borrowing someone else's trending fame.
thedrum.com / famouscampaigns.com / mediapost.com · launched October 28, 2026

Columbia Sportswear gives away a real survival bunker to mock billionaire doomsday prepping

Columbia Sportswear and agency adam&eve\TBWA launched "The Don't Panic Room," a contest offering a real 40-foot off-grid survival bunker, complete with kitchen, bunk beds, bathroom, warm clothing and a robotic dog named Rocky, to whoever best proves outdoor survival skills via video submitted on Instagram or Columbia's campaign site through November 24. The launch ran a New York Times print ad and billboards across Silicon Valley with lines like "Try starting a campfire with crypto or fly fishing with microchips. Good luck with that," aiming squarely at tech-billionaire bunker culture.

Why it mattersInstead of selling gear for an apocalypse scenario, Columbia is selling the idea that real outdoor competence beats buying your way out of a problem, a direct jab at a very specific, very online kind of wealth that most outdoor brands avoid naming out loud.

What is working in content

adweek.com · reported October 29, 2026 · Consumer Edge data cited by bandt.com.au

The Sydney Sweeney effect spikes traffic but keeps failing to produce lasting sales, data suggests

Adweek's review of brand performance after Sydney Sweeney campaigns found the pattern repeating: American Eagle's "Great Jeans" push drove a reported 60% jump in website visits in the days right after launch (Consumer Edge data), but that spike didn't convert into a sustained sales lift, and Dr. Squatch's own Sweeney-fronted stunt showed the same gap between attention and direct sales. Novig has doubled down regardless with a sequel campaign; Adweek's sourced experts frame the pattern as proof that celebrity attention cannot indefinitely cover for weaknesses in a brand's actual product or merchandising.

Why it mattersThis is the data version of the thread running through this whole issue: rented fame generates a real, measurable spike that fades fast, while what a brand already owns, Kimberly-Clark's brands, Tiffany's archive, Asiago's legally defended name, is what the numbers eventually reward.

Social trends

tokchart.com · tracked as of November 3, 2026

"SexyBack" resurfaces after twenty years as TikTok's laziest-to-film trend

  • Justin Timberlake and Timbaland's 2006 single "SexyBack" is adding roughly 46,800 videos a day on TikTok as of November 3, up 69.9% week over week, the fastest-growing large sound tracked that day.
  • The format needs no choreography: creators film themselves lying in bed, letting the song's own energy carry the clip.
  • Maturity: hot and still accelerating.
Why it mattersThe lower the effort required to participate, the faster a sound climbs, and a twenty-year-old song with zero new content behind it is outperforming most fresh drops precisely because anyone can join in thirty seconds, lying down.
tokchart.com, tracked November 3, 2026 / ratingsgamemusic.com, October 30, 2026

A Michael Jackson "Thriller" mashup rides Halloween and the singer's own new TikTok account into a second life

  • "Thriller" (1982) was adding about 28,300 videos a day on TikTok as of November 3, up 59.8% week over week, paired with a parallel spike in Rockwell's 1984 "Somebody's Watching Me" (+61.2%) in a "Somebody's Watching Me x Thriller" mashup format.
  • The song also hit No. 1 on US iTunes ahead of Halloween.
  • The Michael Jackson estate opened an official TikTok account on February 21, 2026, ahead of a biopic, and an AI-powered "Thriller Dance Video Generator" now lets anyone upload a photo and insert themselves as the lead zombie dancer in the choreography.
Why it mattersThis isn't organic nostalgia alone, it's a 44-year-old song getting actively re-platformed by its own rights holder, with an AI tool purpose-built to let fans literally insert themselves into the IP, a more deliberate version of the archive-mining Tiffany is doing with its own history above.

The historical bridge

Roquefort-sur-Soulzon, France · June 4, 1411

A king gave one village the only right to call its cheese by its own name, six hundred years before any court did it for Asiago

On June 4, 1411, King Charles VI of France granted the people of the village of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon a royal monopoly: only cheese aged in their specific limestone caves could be sold under the name "Roquefort," a practice they had already followed for generations. The Parliament of Toulouse reinforced the protection against imitators in 1666. By the time Roquefort became the first French cheese to receive formal Protected Designation of Origin status in 1925, the underlying principle, that a name tied to a specific place is worth defending in law, not just in advertising, was already five centuries old.

Why it still holds. A name only stays valuable if someone is willing to go to court for it, repeatedly, across centuries if needed. Asiago DOP's 2026 win against an "Italian sounding" imitator in the US is the same fight Roquefort's producers were already having in 1411 and again in 1666: defend the name in a courtroom first, then spend the marketing budget telling people why it was worth defending.
